title: Teen Service Star Teaches Coding to Kids Around the World
summary:
At 14, Abhijay Potluri has already started a nonprofit, organized a fundraiser, and taught coding to kids on three continents. The Boxborough, Massachusetts, teen is one of TIME for Kids' Service Stars — and a former TFK Kid Reporter, too.

Abhijay's drive comes from curiosity. "I've always liked knowing how things work," he says. He and his brother used to play I Spy when they were little, and as he got older, he started spotting real problems the same way. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he learned coding and realized kids could build things that help people. That led to Kids Who Teach, a nonprofit where he teaches coding, public speaking, and problem-solving to kids in India, Indonesia, Uganda, and the U.S.

When a fire broke out near his home, Abhijay saw families struggling — some kids in his school became homeless. He wasn't affected himself, but he helped organize a fundraiser anyway. "What stuck with me was seeing every age show up: fourth graders donating next to adults," he says. "It taught me that a small community can make a real difference."

Balancing school, sports, and his projects isn't easy. "Time management" is the biggest challenge, he admits — especially when everything piles up on the same day. But planning his day helps him get things done and still have fun.

Abhijay is bothered by the idea that kids can't make real change because they're young. "That gets to me," he says. But he's living proof otherwise. His proudest moment? Teaching kids in so many different places. "Reaching that many different places is what makes me proudest," he says.

His advice for other kids? Start small. "The hardest part is figuring out where to start," he says. "Once you make a plan or a timeline, it gets a lot easier. You just need to take the first step."
why_it_matters: Abhijay's story is about who gets to learn technology skills: as coding and AI become basic workplace tools, the gap between kids with devices, teachers and internet access and those without becomes a bigger economic divide. It also tests a claim many teenagers hear — that real change waits until adulthood — and suggests the practical limit on youth-led projects is not ideas but time, funding and whether one student's effort can keep going after he graduates.

background_read: TIME for Kids (a news magazine for children published by TIME) chooses 'Service Stars' — young people who volunteer or start projects that help others — and Abhijay is also a former TFK Kid Reporter, one of the children who report and write stories for the magazine. Programs like these are built on the idea that the skills adults use in newsrooms and nonprofits can be practiced long before college.

When COVID-19 closed schools around the world in 2020, huge numbers of students switched to online lessons, and the change exposed a 'digital divide': some kids had laptops and fast internet at home while others shared a single phone or had none. That gap is one reason teaching coding across borders involves more than lessons — students first need a device and a connection.

Uganda (a country in East Africa) has one of the youngest populations in the world, and India and Indonesia both have enormous numbers of school-age children and fast-growing technology industries, so demand for tech skills is high even where trained teachers are scarce. Nonprofits, coding clubs and volunteer teachers try to cover part of that shortage.

Abhijay's hometown, Boxborough, Massachusetts (a small town in the northeastern United States), is where the fire he describes affected local families. Youth-led service is not new — school clubs, scouting groups and bake-sale fundraisers have existed for generations — but the internet now lets a teenager organize and teach across continents from a desk at home.

perspectives.description: Kids in India, Indonesia, Uganda and the United States get free lessons in coding, public speaking and problem-solving from someone close to their own age, which can feel less intimidating than a formal class. The 'kids teaching kids' model is cheap and flexible, and it can reach places where trained computer-science teachers are scarce.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the limits of one teenager's project
perspectives.description: Skeptics note that a single student, however organized, can only teach a small number of children, and short workshops do not replace years of well-funded computer-science instruction in schools. There is also a risk that celebration stories like this one pressure other young people into thinking they must launch an organization to matter, when volunteering locally can be just as useful.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a familiar pattern, with new tools
perspectives.description: Young people have always organized service projects, from school clubs to Scout food drives, and what has changed is the technology: video calls and free coding platforms let a teenager teach across continents. The stumbling block is often infrastructure rather than enthusiasm, because a student who lacks a device or reliable internet cannot join the lesson no matter who is teaching.

As tech skills become requirements in more careers, programs that bring teaching to underserved areas matter more, and the natural next step is training other teenagers to teach so the effort does not depend on one busy student. That connects to Abhijay's own advice — make a plan and take the first step — because the harder second step is building something that survives after its founder moves on.
